articles.title: Amazon’s colorful and sturdy new Kindles
articles.summary: Plus: OpenAI’s Dots, the remastered Witcher 3, Bose’s new wired earbuds, and more.
articles.body: Hi, friends! Welcome to Installer No. 146, your guide to the best and Verge-iest stuff in the world. (If you’re new here, welcome, it’s October already?, and also you can read all the old editions at the Installer homepage.) This week, I’m wishing I could do Walmart potato drone delivery in Portland, watching Mike Tomlin explain his incredible Minecraft city, pondering if the Gears of War pizza cutter is awesome or terrible, exploring Craig Mod’s walks, nodding along with MKBHD’s video about YouTube’s A/B video testing feature, hoping that more concerts ban phones, and celebrating soup season. It’s here! Programming note: David is back next week! It’s been a blast writing Installer again, and thanks to everyone for reading and for your recommendations. For now, I also have for you Amazon’s new Kindles, OpenAI’s Dots, the remastered Witcher 3, and more. (As always, the best part of Installer is your ideas and tips. What apps are you into right now? What are your favorite things you’ve watched / seen / zoned out to recently? Tell me everything: installer@theverge.com. And if you know someone else who might enjoy Installer, forward it to them and tell them to subscribe here.) The Drop * Amazon’s new Kindles. Amazon might have crushed it with the Kindle updates this year. The new base e-readers look like they’ll be a nice upgrade from previous generations, with flush front screens, an option for an aluminum back, and some nice new colors. The new Paperwhite and Colorsoft Signature Editions are compatible with a case with page turn buttons. And now there’s a “Kindle Click” remote to let you turn pages and adjust brightness. My years-old Paperwhite is still trucking along just fine, but if it suddenly broke, these would be really tempting options. * OpenAI’s Dots. OpenAI’s Muse-like AI agent is here, though the company is pitching it more as something to help you with work than an all-encompassing assistant for your personal life. (That’s probably coming later.) The Dots are also adorable, though I think I’d give the Muse mascots the edge in cuteness. * The Witcher 3: Wild Hunt — Remastered. Eleven years after its initial launch, The Witcher 3 is getting yet another big update. This free update for existing owners adds a lot of features and tweaks, including visual improvements, changes to skills, a new accessibility section in settings, cross-platform mod support, and more. The game is also now on Switch 2. Might be time for me to finally dive in. * Bose’s Noise Cancelling Wired Earbuds. These $99 USB-C wired earbuds have noise cancellation and an in-line remote for adjusting volume with a built-in microphone for calls, and they come in three colors. As a huge fan of Apple’s wired EarPods, these could be a great option that’s a step above those in quality. * Ace Combat 8: Wings of Theve. Bandai Namco’s latest entry in its fighter-pilot franchise sounds like a thrilling experience with a campaign filled with optimism, and it’s become one of the best-reviewed games of the year. Seems like a soaring success. * Keurig’s Alta. The new Keurig coffee machine can make you a cup of joe with compostable pucks instead of the recyclable pods. Plus, it can also make espresso and looks super fancy. It’s not cheap at $499.99. But it’s tough to beat the convenience of a Keurig — I learned firsthand when my toddler was a newborn — so this could be a good option if you want to lead a Keurig life with more Earth-friendly pods. * HP’s OmniBook 5 14. This HP laptop is thin and light, has 8GB of RAM, comes in good colors, and starts at $699.99, making it extremely MacBook Neo-adjacent. If you want the Neo ethos paired with Windows, this might be a solid option. * Ikea’s Förlig lamp. This LED Ikea lamp lets you swap between 10 different colors, can be used from the floor or on a wall, and looks kind of like a lightsaber. Super fun. Screen share Today I’m featuring Scott Stein, CNET’s editor at large. I’ve been a huge admirer of Stein’s work, especially his excellent coverage of wearables and VR, for years, and I had the great fortune of finally meeting him in person at Snap and Meta’s events last month. I asked Scott to share his homescreen and the apps and things he cares about. Here it is, plus some info on the apps he uses and why: [Image: The phone: I use an iPhone 16 Pro Max right now. The apps: So I randomize my Home Screen apps. Madness? Maybe. I started doing it for fun by adding suggested Siri app widgets a few years ago. I add two of the widgets, 8 apps each, and then the bottom 8 are fixed ones plus the four on my dock. My fixed ones are: Google Calendar, Photos, Notes, Camera, Music, Gmail, GMaps, Bluesky, Phone, Messages, Mail, Safari. My core go-tos. But the others are a contextual-slash-frequency-based mix of things I might be using (or not). The locations shift. In some ways it’s like Home Screen gaslighting… but it’s also a living Black Mirror life, and often it’s actually helpful. Today there’s the United app since I’m flying, Uber, Siri, Voice Memos, Signal, GChat, YouTube, Asana, Yahoo Sports… mostly pretty useful. The wallpaper: My background’s also randomized. I pull from family and trip photos so I can see my kids (and other odd moments) when I’m out and about. It comforts me. I also asked Scott to share a few things he’s into right now. Here’s what he sent back: The apps: * I have had an ongoing magic hobby since I was a kid. I’m reading The Intuitive Magician: Mastering Magic Through Improvisation, by Justin Higham. Kind of technical but it’s an exploration of where practice and fluid improvising meet, which feels holistic for other things. * Also reading Stephen King and Peter Straub’s Black House, after reading The Talisman. I loved the Dark Tower books and the new Talisman trilogy end is coming soon which apparently blends them all together. * I’ve also been semi obsessed with runes lately, part of my interest in portable trinkets and talismans, and how readings can feel like a form of meditation. * Still playing Fire Emblem: Fortune’s Weave, and carving out time ahead for Panic Playdate’s third season. I love that little handheld. Crowdsourced Here’s what the Installer community is into this week. I want to know what you’re into right now as well! Email installer@theverge.com with your recommendations for anything and everything, and we’ll feature some of our favorites here every week. For even more great recommendations, check out the replies to this post on The Verge. “Arc Raiders (Expedition done and 2.0 coming in a week!) and Control Resonant. East of Eden.” — ProtoPhil “I just started Widow’s Bay last night. Currently reading The Velvet Rage. Listening to the new Orville Peck album, Madonna, Adele, Amy Winehouse. Playing Stardew Valley. — antwhat “Started watching American Horror Story: 13 and the first three episodes were pretty interesting! Love seeing the old characters’ reunion.” — alee “I’m watching Star Trek: Voyager again! Light, serious, funny and introspective, a great watch in a time where the AI news has been a serious of scary headlines.” — BlubberBacon “I’ve got a stack of spooky season reading that I can’t wait to dig into: The Nudge by Joseph Fink, Breakable Things and The Salt Grows Heavy by Cassandra Khaw, and The King in Yellow by Robert Chambers (Cthulhu’s grandpappy).” — Barbarian Librarian “I’m playing Antivirus Survivors 2003 Professional because I’m apparently an ‘unc’ gamer.” — bubble_boy “Two separate reading recommendations: Andrew Sacher’s Emo Revival and Tress of the Emerald Sea by Brandon Sanderson. Loved them both.” — securingsincity “The latest episode of South Park America was brilliant!” — verge_user_BlorpBlorp Signing off Remember my minimal homescreen I showed off in my first issue I wrote back in August? I have to confess: It became a mess of apps during my travels this month. Multiple airline apps, an expense reporting app, Notes, Voice Memos, Uber, and more — it gave me hives. Fortunately, I’ve finally gotten around to cleaning things up, and the screen is back down to just the Messages app once again. Calm restored. Well, until my next trip. See you around!

articles.title: The rise, fall, and rise of portable MP3 players
articles.summary: ﻿Apple perfected the media player with the iPod, then abandoned it.
articles.body: This is The Stepback, a weekly newsletter breaking down one essential story from the tech world. For more on the collapse and the resurgence of the portable media player, follow Terrence O’Brien. The Stepback arrives in our subscribers’ inboxes on Sunday at 8AM ET. Opt in for The Stepback here. How it started We are spoiled for choice, musically. Most of us walk around with access to hundreds of millions of songs in our pockets. But it wasn’t until 1998 that portable digital music was even a thing. Before that we lugged booklets full of CDs on the bus or stashed a handful of cassettes in our backpacks. With the advent of the MP3 player in the 2000s we were soon able to carry massive libraries of music everywhere we went — over 1,000 albums’ worth depending on the file format and the size of your MP3 player. The MPMan F10 is generally considered to be the first commercial MP3 player. It was roughly the size of a deck of cards and looked like an oversized pager. It launched in Asia in March of 1998, but it barely made a blip on anyone’s radar. It was the Diamond Rio PMP300 that broke through in the West a few months later, in September of 1998. It was slightly larger, and its design more closely resembles what we envision when we think of a media player (namely the iPod). But even then, it drew more attention because the Recording Industry Association of America (RIAA) sued Diamond Multimedia in an attempt to stop the spread of MP3s. The F10 and the PMP300 were, unsurprisingly, primitive by today’s standards, shipping with just 32MB — yes, that’s megabytes — of storage. That tiny amount of built-in memory only allowed for around 12 songs to be stored on them. They held less audio than a CD and generally sounded worse. But it wasn’t that big of a limitation, in comparison to the nightmare that was the UI on their tiny monochrome LCDs. Plus, you could expand storage on both using SmartMedia cards if you really needed to. Eventually, some companies addressed the storage issue by swapping flash storage, which was still relatively limited at the time, for traditional spinning-disc hard drives. The Creative Nomad Jukebox, for instance, had a 6GB drive inside. It also had a more familiar design modeled after portable CD players. But that made it bulkier than the competition; it weighed a shocking 14 ounces. Unsurprisingly, it also failed to usher MP3 players into the mainstream. It wasn’t until the introduction of the iPod in November 2001 that the golden age of portable media players truly took off. By 2007, roughly 20 percent of Americans owned a personal media player. Other companies, including Microsoft and Creative, tried to carve out space for themselves with Zune and Zen lines, respectively. But Apple’s iPod was the dominant force in the market, accounting for over 70 percent of media player sales. While 20 percent isn’t ubiquitous, the iPod and the digital music revolution certainly felt inescapable in the 2000s. Bands like Radiohead and Nine Inch Nails were experimenting with pay-what-you-want digital releases. Napster taught everyone the phrases “file sharing” and “peer-to-peer.” And Apple’s iconic ads combining silhouettes and white earbuds were everywhere. The personal media player’s spotlight was relatively short-lived. While Apple didn’t fully discontinue the iPod lineup until 2022, it retired the Classic model in 2014 and cut the Nano and Shuffle in 2017, leaving the iPod Touch — essentially an iPhone without the phone — as the last iPod standing. By 2011, the writing was on the wall as iPhone sales eclipsed iPod sales for the first time. The portable media player market shrank quickly as modern smartphones replaced flip phones and BlackBerrys, and music consumption moved away from purchasing CDs or digital downloads toward streaming. What was, at its peak, a $21.6 billion industry in 2008 had collapsed to just $613 million in 2012, according to research firm Mintel. How it’s going It’s difficult to get reliable numbers for the size of the digital audio player market these days. Some research firms lump all media players together, regardless of whether they’re audio or video, streaming or offline. Others that do track audio-specific players as a separate market segment can’t seem to agree. Some report that it’s a $180 million-plus industry on the rise. Others say it’s only a $1.2 million market and it’s shrinking. One thing is certain, though: Portable media players have become a very small niche. For most of the last 10 years, dedicated portable music players were primarily the realm of audiophiles. Companies like Sony and Astell & Kern have been steadily releasing high-end audio players that can sell for well north of $3,000. Sony’s NW-A306 is the only device offered by either company that even approaches a mainstream consumer price, at $399.99. These devices aren’t just more expensive, they’re more complicated than the iPods of yore. Wi-Fi and Bluetooth are a given. They feature large touchscreens and high-end digital audio converters. They also often run Android, opening them up to streaming apps like Spotify and Qobuz. Sony has fully embraced the iPod Touch model, giving its players full access to the Google Play store. The sky-high prices and embrace of apps has led many to reject these players. Instead, those looking for an offline listening experience free from notifications and algorithms have turned to the past. Vintage iPods still fetch hundreds of dollars on eBay. An entire cottage industry has cropped up around modding them — adding modern features like Bluetooth and USB-C, replacing the dying hard drives and batteries, or just customizing the appearance. What happens next As popular as the iPod was, the world’s supply of working used units will eventually run out. As they age, batteries will stop holding a charge and spinning drives will fail, and most people don’t want to open up a piece of delicate electronics or mess with a soldering iron. But the renewed interest in iPods is starting to drive up prices on other media players, and modders are now swapping new drives into Zunes and selling them for hundred of dollars on eBay. With Google searches for “MP3 player” nearly tripling since last year and The New York Times running trend pieces about the iPod resurgence, a number of companies and startups are trying to cash in. Chinese manufacturers have flooded AliExpress, Temu, and Amazon with a ton of dirt-cheap players and shameless iPod knockoffs. Wildly successful crowdfunding campaigns, like that of the AP30 Music Boy, show there is pent-up demand for retro portable music players. But most out there aren’t moving the needle much in terms of design or usability. Sleevenote is one startup that’s attempting to break the mold, but its success is far from guaranteed. It’s a startup from musician Tom Vek that embraces some modern conveniences like syncing over Wi-Fi and Bluetooth headphones, but skips on any extraneous features like streaming, apps, or games. It swaps scrolling text lists of artist names for a grid of album art. It’s highly visual, and attempts to re-create the experience of paging through a CD booklet. It also has limited integration with a host of digital music storefronts like Bandcamp, Subvert, Bleep, Qobuz, Amazon Music, and more. Vek has a promising-looking concept on its hands that actually approaches the portable media player in a fresh way. But the bulky Day One edition still has a lot of kinks to work out, including disappointing battery life. (I’ve been testing one for a couple of months now.) Plus, it’s currently sold out and the company doesn’t know when the next batch will be made available. There’s growing anti-streaming sentiment, and the slowtech trend doesn’t seem to be going anywhere anytime soon. But no obvious heir to the iPod throne has stepped in to fill the gap in the MP3 player market. It seems unlikely that the MP3 player will see a resurgence on the scale of vinyl or even CDs. In part because, for whatever convenience advantage an iPod might have over a limited edition LP, it lacks the collectibility factor. And that has been a major driver of the physical media resurgence, as evidenced by the fact that, while Gen Z and millennials might be buying up CDs in record numbers, half of them don’t own a CD player. By the way * Suzanne Vega is sometimes called the “mother of the MP3.” Karlheinz Brandenburg was working on audio compression technology at the Fraunhofer Society (FHG) in Germany and turned to Vega’s “Tom’s Diner” as his benchmark due to her “warm, human voice” that would be a challenge to encode. Thousands of miles away, James Johnston also turned to “Tom’s Diner” while working on audio compression at Bell Labs. Brandenburg and Johnston’s work ultimately led to the creation of MPEG-1 Audio Layer III standard, better known as MP3. * Kane Kramer is widely credited with inventing the first digital audio player in 1979, and successfully patented it in the UK in 1985, and the US in 1987. Many of its features, including an online music store, would eventually find their way into the iPod and iTunes. And Paul McCartney was an early financial backer, but his IXI never saw a commercial release. Kramer’s patents lapsed in 1988. While Apple eventually gave him credit for his invention, it was primarily a legal maneuver to undermine a company called Burst.com that sued Apple for patent infringement. Read this * Brandon Shaw, host of YouTube channel Digging the Greats, ditched streaming for an iPod two years ago and documented the experience over the course of several videos. * The New York Times looked at how younger generations were embracing old-school media formats, including the iPod, in an attempt to break free of the shackles of streaming. * The Verge crew shared their fond memories of the iPod when Apple officially put it out to pasture in 2022. * This visual history of the iPod charts its evolution from clunky brick to sleek icon of modern design.

articles.title: The iPad Mini is slightly cheaper again during Prime Day
articles.summary: October Prime Day is bringing down the price on the iPad Mini with the A17 Pro chip.
articles.body: Apple bumped up prices on several of its devices in June, and we haven’t seen a good discount on the iPad Mini since. Just ahead of Amazon’s October Prime Big Deals Days, however, both Wi-Fi only and cellular-connected models are $100 off. The Wi-Fi version with 128GB of storage is currently $499, the 256GB model is $599, and the cellular model with 128GB of storage is $649. This base configuration of this tablet often sold for around $400 throughout 2025, so we get it if $500 for a tablet from late 2024 is still too much. But it’s the best price since late June, and if there’s a new version coming out later this year, it might be significantly more expensive. [Product: iPad Mini (2024) | We reviewed this version of the iPad Mini when it launched in 2024, and while we appreciated the processor upgrade and Apple Intelligence features, it felt lacking in some of the quality-of-life improvements found in the larger iPads that launched around the same time. Read our Apple iPad Mini (2024) review.

articles.title: The AirPods Pro 3 are a fantastic deal at $179
articles.summary: For Amazon’s October Prime Day, you can snag a $70 discount on the Apple AirPods Pro 3 wireless earbuds.
articles.body: It’s been a while since we’ve seen a good discount on the Apple AirPods Pro 3, but like the latest iPad Mini and the M5 MacBook Airs, a great one is happening now for October Prime Day. You can snag a pair of the noise-canceling earbuds that include five ear tip sizes, live translation, and fantastic sound for $179 at Amazon (originally $249). I expect other retailers to offer a similar price in the coming days. This is the first time the price has gone below $190 since Prime Day in June. Since then, Apple launched the AirPods 5, and the most feature-complete version with a wireless charging case costs $149.99. Those are great if you prefer earbuds that don’t form a seal in your ears, but for everyone else, the AirPods Pro 3 are a much better value at just $30 more right now. [Product: AirPods Pro 3 | Read our AirPods Pro 3 review.

articles.title: This toolless modular lever-action wallet is the coolest I’ve stuck to my phone
articles.summary: The OhSnap Wallet 2 is a lever-action aluminum wallet with stackable modular parts, so a three card pocket wallet can transform into a seven card magnet one!
articles.body: This toolless modular lever-action wallet is the coolest I’ve stuck to my phone. Remember when I tested the ultra-thin and convenient OhSnap Snap Grip Stand and liked it so much I bought my own? Now, OhSnap has a magnetic lever-action card wallet that can stack with that stand. It’s the coolest wallet I’ve ever stuck to my phone. [Media: Pull the integrated springy lever, and your cards fan out. Want a thicker or thinner wallet? Press in the right place and it comes apart without tools, letting you swap in a 3, 5, or 7-card “core” that grips your cards so they don’t fall out. Want an ID card, work badge, elastic band for more cards, or a money clip on the end? You can change out the front or back magnetic plates for any of those. Or, change out both for ultra-thin aluminum covers if you don’t need the wallet to magnetically stick to your phone. You can see it in action in my Today I’m Toying With video embedded in this post (also on YouTube and on Instagram if you prefer). My favorite part is that the whole kit snaps together using a compliant mechanism — the plastic arms of the card-carrying core act like springs, pushing a little locking mechanism into the notches of each modular cover you add as you slide the parts together. Once your cards are inside, they keep the arms apart so it can’t open accidentally (unless you drop the entire wallet). It’s all very clever. [Image: With the ID card holder attached, and the core mounted to put the lever up instead of down. Even when I did drop the wallet (thanks for the suggestion, hugo!), it didn’t explode, typically. Usually, it just came apart slightly, though I did drop it hard on concrete one time and was able to make a small explosion: one half popped off, and two cards came out, but everything landed in a two-foot radius. The wallet has a big dent now. There are definitely some downsides. While OhSnap advertises the Wallet 2 as “impossibly thin,” it’s only truly surprisingly sleek in its thinnest 3-card variant, without the thicker and heavier MagSafe and MagStack (which lets you snap other magnets to it) plates attached. But the reason I’m not buying one is the price and weight. The 7-card version makes my phone feel too heavy, adding 127 grams, and while I happily made the 3-card my wallet for a few weeks, it’d cost me $61 on Kickstarter or $76 retail to get that with a double-magnet kit. OhSnap’s also charging more than I’d like ($35 for an ID cover or a money clip!) for extras. [Image: [Image: OhSnap didn’t get me this time. But I could see giving one as a present.

articles.title: Yeh Rishta Kya Kehlata Hai fame Mohsin Khan gets married to Tamanna; shares a dreamy glimpse
articles.summary: Yeh Rishta Kya Kehlata Hai actor Mohsin Khan has sparked wedding buzz after sharing a glimpse from what appears to be his wedding celebrations with
articles.body: Yeh Rishta Kya Kehlata Hai actor Mohsin Khan has sparked wedding buzz after sharing a glimpse from what appears to be his wedding celebrations with Tamanna. The actor shared a picture with Tamanna and captioned it, “The Day MashaAllah.”In the picture, Mohsin can be seen dressed in a white and black suit, while Tamanna looks beautiful in a traditional multicultural outfit. The couple appears to be enjoying their special day as they pose together.Soon after Mohsin shared the post, several clips from the celebrations started doing the rounds on social media. In the videos, Mohsin and Tamanna can be seen dancing and enjoying themselves with their loved ones. The happy moments have caught the attention of fans, who have been showering the couple with congratulatory messages.Mohsin and Tamanna had got engaged in August this year. Sharing pictures from their engagement, the actor had penned a heartfelt note and called Tamanna his “Person”.“The first time we looked at each other, the first time I held your hand to the first time you sang ‘Hum toh bhai jaise hai waise rahenge’, I knew something within me settled. I had found my Person,” he had written.Mohsin is best known for playing Kartik Goenka in Yeh Rishta Kya Kehlata Hai. His pairing with Shivangi Joshi in the show became hugely popular among television audiences.Get the latest TV News, TV Shows and more. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: Khatron Ke Khiladi 15 Winner: Avinash Mishra lifts the trophy; takes home Rs 20 lakh cash prize
articles.summary: After months of performing difficult and dangerous stunts, TV actor Avinash Mishra emerged as the winner of Khatron Ke Khiladi 15.
articles.body: After months of performing difficult and dangerous stunts, TV actor Avinash Mishra emerged as the winner of Khatron Ke Khiladi 15. The stunt-based reality show which took a break last year, returned after a highly anticipated two-year hiatus. Hosted by the action king Rohit Shetty, the season ended with Avinash Mishra being crowned the winner and Rithvik Dhanjani and Orhan Awatramani (Orry), emerging as the first and second runners-up, respectively. Season 15 was shot in the breathtaking terrains of Cape Town and introduced the high voltage ‘Champions vs. Challengers’ format. The Champions vs. Challengers saw the franchise veterans pitted against fresh contenders.The season featured scary machine stunts, the most discussed tough ‘Pain Auction’ task, Darr Ka Naya Daur which brought new challenges every week and kept viewers entertained.During the season, Avinash Mishra went from being a new contestant to one of the strongest performers. He proved that he was more than just a good-looking TV actor. His strong mindset and excellent stunt skills helped him stand out. He also gave several impressive performances during the show. As soon as host Rohit Shetty announced Avinash's name as the winner, the actor broke down in tears. Avinash told Rohit Shetty, "In the last 10 years, I've been nominated for several characters and have attended award functions, but this is the first time, I'm winning an award."After lifting the trophy, Avinash ran towards close friend Eisha Singh, who was sitting in the audience and hugged her tightly. The duo celebrated the occasion and were also seen getting teary-eyed.Avinash opens up about winner KKK 15Sharing his gratitude, Avinash Mishra said, “Winning Khatron Ke Khiladi feels special because I thought I signed up for the show with a point to prove, but along the way, the person I ended up proving it to, was myself. I have spent years being associated with television and, yes, with being the good-looking guy on screen. I enjoyed that journey, but I also knew there was so much more I wanted people to see in me. This show gave me the chance to put everything else aside and literally let my actions speak. Most of this journey was actually about the mind. You can prepare yourself physically, but when you are standing at the edge of something terrifying, there is no performance left – it is just you, your fear and the decision you make in that moment. I had to learn to tune out the noise, trust myself, and keep going. There were days when I surprised myself, and those are the moments I will cherish. And to win the show after everything I have discovered about myself here is the kind of ending I could only have hoped for. I came to Khatron Ke Khiladi wanting to test myself; I am leaving with a belief in myself that I didn’t have before. That, for me, is the biggest victory.”During the high-octane Team Week twist, he was appointed Team Captain and strategically steered his rookie squad entirely out of danger against a veteran-heavy team led by Rithvik Dhanjani. His fearless execution across dizzying heights and heavy machinery tasks earned him praise, and a highly coveted, signed custom Fear Jacket from Rohit Shetty. Avinash’s defining breakthrough arrived during a technically demanding, high-pressure underwater task, where he outperformed seasoned veteran Karan Wahi to claim a spot as the season’s very first Top 5 Finalist. His remarkable evolution culminated in an epic Grand Finale showdown, where Avinash conquered the ultimate helicopter-to-water stunt to emerge victoriously, taking home the coveted trophy, Rs 20 lakh cash prize and a brand-new car.Get the latest TV News, TV Shows and more. articles.title: Bigg Boss Kannada 13: Agnipariksha contestant Likith Gondhi gets evicted, says, "Life was good, is good, and will be good"
articles.summary: The latest weekend episode of Bigg Boss Kannada 13 witnessed an unexpected turn of events as contestant Likith Gondhi was shown the exit door following a
articles.body: The latest weekend episode of Bigg Boss Kannada 13 witnessed an unexpected turn of events as contestant Likith Gondhi was shown the exit door following a dramatic elimination segment. His eviction marks the end of a rather eventful journey inside the Bigg Boss house, one filled with fun, rebellion, entertaining moments and occasional clashes.Likith's journey in the reality show has been anything but ordinary. He entered the house as a commoner through the challenging Agnipariksha route and gradually made his presence felt among the contestants. From his playful antics and mischievous behaviour to his outspoken nature and rebellious streak, Likith managed to create his own identity in the house. His unpredictable approach to tasks, interactions with fellow contestants and occasional outbursts kept viewers entertained throughout his stint.Following his eviction, Likith joined host Kiccha Sudeep on stage, where they discussed his journey and the circumstances surrounding his elimination.Speaking about his eviction, Likith admitted that he had somewhat anticipated the outcome. He acknowledged that his anger issues and a dip in his performance over the past week could have worked against him. Despite the disappointment, he maintained a positive outlook and expressed gratitude for the experience and the support he received from viewers.Putting things into perspective, Likith shared an optimistic message: "Life was good, is good, and will be good." He also thanked everyone who supported him throughout his Bigg Boss journey, acknowledging the love and encouragement he received from the audience.Adding a touch of humour to the conversation, Sudeep playfully described Likith's journey as a 'monkeying' one, seemingly referring to his mischievous, energetic and sometimes unpredictable behaviour inside the house. The light-hearted exchange brought some fun to the eviction segment, offering viewers a glimpse of Likith's entertaining side even as he bid farewell to the show.While his journey may have come to an end, Likith leaves behind several memorable moments, controversies and entertaining episodes. His eviction is another significant development in Bigg Boss Kannada 13, as the competition gets tougher and the remaining contestants move closer to the ultimate title.For Likith, the Bigg Boss chapter closes on a positive note, with his belief in better days ahead reflecting his spirited approach to life beyond the house.Get the latest TV News, TV Shows and more.
